title: Runtime Profiling Playbook: Systemic Steps for Low-Latency Investigations
author: Marina Chen
content:
Overview:

Purpose:
This playbook explains how to profile and triage runtime-level performance regressions (high p95/p99 latency, sudden throughput drops, GPU underutilization, and kernel scheduling anomalies) for the Redwood serving runtime. It is a pragmatic, step-by-step guide for oncall and SRE/RT engineers to collect repeatable artifacts, interpret them, and enact mitigations or rollbacks.

Scope:
- Applies to Redwood Hosted and Dedicated runtime clusters running redwood-runtime v1.6+ (including batcher, kv-cache, rpc-proxy, and serve-gpu-agent).
- Focused on inference-serving performance: generation latencies, KV cache hotspots, batching behavior, and kernel scheduling on GPU hosts.
- Not a model-quality playbook (see eval-harness docs for prompt/regression checks).

Quick summary:
- If tail latency spike observed: collect traces (jaeger/x-ray), profiling sampling (perf/NSYS), GPU metrics (nvidia-smi / DCGM / Prometheus), and runtime traces (redwood-trace).
- Correlate with recent deploys, kernel/driver updates, and autoscaler events.
- If kernel stalls detected, isolate at host-level and pin offending container to a maintenance pool or rollback to previous runtime image.

Owner and escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (runtime-performance subteam)
- First escalation: Runtime Performance lead (Diego Alvarez)
- SLA for incident classification: triage within 15 minutes during business hours / 60 minutes off-hours.

Required access and prerequisites:
- Kube cluster view and logs (cluster-reader), access to grafana and prometheus, and read access to DCGM metrics collector.
- SSH to GPU hosts (for full-system traces) requires security approval.
- Local tools: perf (v5+), nsight-systems (nsys), pprof or flamegraph scripts, jq, kubectl, and redwood-cli.

Collect fast artifacts (first 10 minutes):
1) High-level indicators:
- Grafana dashboard link (SLO dashboard): /grafana/d/redwood-runtime/perf-overview
- Record SLO violations (p95/p99, tokens/sec, queue length) and the time window.
2) Runtime logs:
- kubectl -n redwood logs deployment/batcher --since=15m --tail=200 > batcher.log
- kubectl -n redwood logs deployment/serve-gpu-agent --since=15m --tail=200 > agent.log
3) Traces and spans:
- Use redwood-trace UI or query Jaeger: service=batcher AND operation=generate AND duration>=100ms
- Download trace JSON for a representative p99 request.
4) GPU and host metrics:
- kubectl top nodes; DCGM exporter: curl http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=dcgm_sm_active_pct
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,compute_mode --format=csv -l 1 (run for 30s)
5) Lightweight profiling sampling:
- On the container: kill -USR1 $(pidof redwood-runtime) if configured to dump pstack (opt-in) OR run perf top in a short sampling window: perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 8; perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.folded

Deep-dive procedures

A. Reproducing the regression (isolated experiment):
1) Pin a single model and request path that reproduces the tail latency locally or in a canary nodepool.
2) Use the redwood-load tool to replay recorded traces at 1x/2x QPS to observe whether hard limits or queue buildup occurs:
- redwood-cli load --trace-file example-trace.json --concurrency 4 --duration 120s --target endpoint://model/fn
3) If reproducible in canary, snapshot kube events, container config, and the node's driver/kernel versions:
- kubectl get nodes -o wide; uname -sr; cat /etc/os-release; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version --format=csv

B. Kernel scheduling / host-level checks (how to detect and triage):
Indicators for kernel scheduling problems:
- High p99 with low GPU SM utilization and high CPU sys% or iowait.
- Frequent context switches, high softirq, or kernel preemption events visible in dmesg (e.g., thrashing or page faults).
- perf record shows many kernel stacks (vs user stacks) and system call hotspots (copy_from_user, sched_hung_task, wake_up_new_task).

Host isolation steps:
1) Check dmesg for driver/kernel warnings: ssh node; sudo journalctl -k --since "15 minutes ago" | tail -n 200
2) Collect perf for kernel events: sudo perf record -e sched:sched_switch -a -- sleep 10; sudo perf script > sched-switch.txt
3) If kernel busy, try to repro on a fresh node (same instance type, AMI). If fresh node is fine, suspect node-level corruption (memory, driver).
4) For suspected GPU driver regressions: verify driver version against known-good matrix (see appendix). If node shows a newer driver pushed via image, roll the nodepool to previous AMI.

C. GPU kernel stalls and long GPU memcpy times:
- Symptoms: high GPU utilization but low achieved throughput; long memcpy times visible in Nsight traces.
- Capture NSYS system-wide timeline on the node where the container runs: sudo nsys profile --output=/tmp/nsys-profile --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi -w true --wait=10 -p 1 -t none --trace=cuda,osrt --force-overwrite -- sleep 8
- Convert to report: nsys stats /tmp/nsys-profile.qdrep --report gtcuda
- Look for long gaps between kernel launches, excessive cudaMemcpy or cudaMemcpyAsync durations, and large host-side stalls.

D. Batcher and KV cache contention checks:
- Batcher metrics: queue_length, batch_encoding_ms, dispatch_ms, batch_size_histogram
- KV cache: cache_hit_rate, cache_evictions_per_min, kv_serialize_ms
- Prometheus queries (examples):
  - rate(redwood_batcher_queue_length[1m])
  - histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(redwood_batcher_dispatch_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  - sum(rate(redwood_kv_evictions_total[5m])) by (node)
- If batcher queue grows and batch size drops, suspect per-request head-of-line blocking or synchronous preprocessing.

E. Profiling at the runtime binary level (GNU/linux containers):
- Build a minimal repro image with debug symbols (redwood-runtime-debug) and run under perf and gdb if needed.
- perf record -F 200 -g -p <pid> -- sleep 15; perf report --call-graph
- For memory alloc hotspots use: heaptrack or jemalloc profiling (if using jemalloc: MALLOC_CONF=prof:true,lg_sample:16 jeprof)

Runbook: step-by-step for an active incident (fast checklist)
1) Validate: Confirm alert system and correlate with user reports and Grafana.
2) Scope: Identify affected customers/tenants, models, regions, nodepools.
3) Stabilize: Redirect traffic to fallback pool/previous image or increase capacity to absorb load (if safe).
4) Collect: Follow the fast-artifact checklist above.
5) Diagnose: Use A/B (canary) repro steps and kernel scheduling checks.
6) Mitigate: If host-level, cordon node and drain; if runtime-level, roll back runtime image; if GPU driver, revert AMI or driver package.
7) Post-incident: Attach artifacts to incident ticket and create a follow-up action item with owner and due date.

Mitigations with command examples:
- Cordon and drain node: kubectl cordon NODE && kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- Roll runtime Deployment: kubectl -n redwood set image deployment/serve-gpu-agent serve-gpu-agent=ghcr.io/redwood/release/redwood-runtime:v1.5.9
- Reallocate traffic by scaling down canary: kubectl -n redwood scale deploy/serve-gpu-agent --replicas=0 && scale back to 4 replicas in fallback pool.

When to rollback vs mitigations:
- Rollback if a single recent runtime or driver change correlates with the start of the regression and repro is successful on a previous image.
- Apply mitigations (drain nodes, increase capacity) if underlying cause is unknown or customer-facing impact is large and a rollback risks more instability.

Performance validation matrix (what to collect after fix):
- Run the standard perf-suite job for the failing endpoint: benchmarks/serve/latency/trace-driven-job.yaml (example below).
- Validate SLOs over 1h: p95 <= 120ms for small model (<1B tokens/sec baseline), p99 <= 300ms for long tail scenarios (config-dependent), throughput within +/- 5% of pre-incident baseline.

Example benchmark job (trace-driven, short):
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: runtime-perf-smoke
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: loader
        image: ghcr.io/redwood/tools/redwood-load:stable
        args: ["--trace-file","/traces/smoke.json","--concurrency","8","--duration","180"]
      restartPolicy: Never
  backoffLimit: 0
---

Appendix: useful Prometheus queries and traces
- Node-level context switch spike: rate(node_context_switches_total[5m])
- GPU memcpy backlog: avg_over_time(dcgm_gpu_memory_copy_time_ms[5m])
- Batch queue length by model: sum(redwood_batcher_queue_length{model=~".*"}) by (model)

Troubleshooting table (common symptoms -> likely causes -> first action):
- Symptom: high p99, low GPU util -> Causes: kernel scheduling, driver regression, host I/O -> Action: collect dmesg; perf sched; nsys timeline; cordon node
- Symptom: high GPU util, low throughput -> Causes: memcpy stalls, small kernels launch overhead -> Action: nsys capture; check batch sizing and host memory bandwidth
- Symptom: intermittent spikes on single tenant -> Causes: noisy neighbor, cache eviction -> Action: inspect tenant metrics; isolate to dedicated nodepool

FAQ and notes:
- Q: Can we run nsys in production? A: Yes, but only on canary/maintenance nodes. NSYS can add overhead; prefer short captures and off-host repro runs for long traces.
- Q: Are jemalloc profiles safe to collect? A: Use debug instances; jemalloc profiling has memory and CPU overhead and should not be enabled by default on production stable pools.

Follow-ups and runbook grooming:
- After any incident where kernel scheduling or driver issues were suspected, create a follow-up ADR recommending a driver gating policy and node AMI pinning for critical nodepools.
- Maintain a driver-to-runtime compatibility matrix in this directory (related_pages below).
